verses.text: Then the people and their wives raised a loud outcry against their fellow Jews.
Some said, “There are a lot of us, with all our sons and daughters. We need grain so we can eat and stay alive.”
Others said, “We’re putting up our fields, vineyards, and houses as security just to get grain in this famine.”
Still others said, “We’ve borrowed money to pay the king’s tax, putting up our fields and vineyards as collateral.

We’re flesh and blood just like our fellow Jews, and our children are just like theirs. Yet we’re having to send our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, and there’s nothing we can do about it. Other people have our fields and vineyards.”
When I heard their outcry and what they were saying, I got really angry.
I thought it over, then confronted the nobles and officials. I said, “You’re charging interest to your own people!” I called a big assembly to bring the charges against them.

I told them, “As far as we could, we bought back our fellow Jews who’d been sold to other nations. Now you’re selling your own people, so we have to buy them back from you?” They went quiet and couldn’t find a word to say.
I went on, “What you’re doing is wrong. Shouldn’t you live in reverence for our God and keep our enemies, the other nations, from mocking us?
My brothers, my servants, and I are lending them money and grain too. Please, let’s stop charging this interest.
Give them back their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses today. Give back the hundredth part of the money, grain, new wine, and oil you’ve been charging them.”
They said, “We’ll give it all back and demand nothing from them. We’ll do exactly what you say.” So I called the priests and made the nobles and officials swear to keep their promise.

I also shook out the fold of my robe and said, “May God shake anyone who breaks this promise out of their home and away from everything they’ve worked for. May they be shaken out and left empty like this.” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. The people kept their promise.
From the time I was appointed governor in Judah, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, twelve years in all, my brothers and I didn’t take the governor’s food allowance.

The governors before me lived at the people’s expense. They took bread and wine from them, plus forty shekels of silver. Even their servants bossed the people around. I didn’t do that because I feared God.
I stuck with the work on this wall. We didn’t buy any land, and all my servants gathered there to work.
I had 150 Jewish men and officials at my table, besides those who came to us from the nations around us.

Every day one ox, six choice sheep, and some birds were prepared for me. Every ten days there was a fresh supply of all kinds of wine. Even with all that, I didn’t demand the governor’s allowance because the burden on these people was already heavy.
Remember me, my God, for all the good I’ve done for these people.
